reminder: An additive function $f$ satisfies $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ whenever $m$ and $n$ are [coprime](c:coprime-integers).
definition: An [arithmetic function](c:arithmetic-function) $f$ is additive when $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ for all [coprime](c:coprime-integers) positive integers $m$ and $n$. It is completely additive when this holds for all positive integers $m$ and $n$.
examples: $\omega(n)$, the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, is additive.
$\log n$ and $\Omega(n)$, the number of prime divisors counted with multiplicity, are completely additive.
Non-example: $f(n)=n$ is not additive, because $f(2\cdot3)=6$ but $f(2)+f(3)=5$.

steps: Take an additive function $f$.
Its inputs are positive integers and its values are numbers, so $f$ is an [arithmetic function](c:arithmetic-function).
The additive case adds the rule $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ for [coprime](c:coprime-integers) $m$ and $n$.
links.why: It shows that additivity is one extra rule on a function of the positive integers.

reminder: An untwisted affine Lie algebra is a [central extension](c:central-extension) of the [loop algebra](c:loop-algebra) of a simple Lie algebra.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional simple [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) with invariant form $(\cdot,\cdot)$. The [loop algebra](c:loop-algebra) $\mathfrak g\otimes\mathbb C[t,t^{-1}]$ has a [central extension](c:central-extension) $\hat{\mathfrak g}$ with a central element $K$ and bracket $[x\otimes t^m,y\otimes t^n]=[x,y]\otimes t^{m+n}+m\,\delta_{m+n,0}(x,y)K$. This is the untwisted affine Lie algebra, a [Kac-Moody algebra](c:kac-moody-algebra) of affine type.
examples: For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, the algebra $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2$ has basis $e_m,f_m,h_m$ for $m\in\mathbb Z$ and the central element $K$.
In an irreducible highest weight representation, the central element $K$ acts as a number $k$, the level.
Non-example: $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ is not affine, because it is finite-dimensional and every affine Lie algebra is infinite-dimensional.

steps: Take the generalized Cartan matrix $A$ of the affine Lie algebra $\hat{\mathfrak g}$.
A [Kac-Moody algebra](c:kac-moody-algebra) is built from a generalized Cartan matrix by Chevalley generators and Serre relations.
Affine type adds the condition that $A$ is indecomposable, positive semidefinite and singular.
links.why: It shows that affine Lie algebras are the Kac-Moody algebras whose Cartan matrix has corank one.

reminder: An affine subspace is the empty set or a point plus a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace).
definition: Let $P$ be an [affine space](c:affine-space) with direction [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $k$. A subset $S\subseteq P$ is an affine subspace when $S$ is empty or when $S=p+W$ for a point $p\in P$ and a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) $W$ of $V$. Equivalently, $S$ contains every affine combination of its points.
examples: Every line in the plane is an affine subspace, also a line that does not pass through the origin.
The solution set of $Ax=b$ in $k^n$ is an affine subspace when it is not empty. Its direction is the kernel of $A$.
Non-example: the unit circle in $\mathbb R^2$ is not an affine subspace, because the line through two of its points leaves the circle.

steps: Let $W$ be a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) of $V$, seen as a subset of the affine space $V$.
It contains $0$, so $W=0+W$ is a point plus a linear subspace.
Hence $W$ is an affine subspace with direction $W$.
Conversely, an affine subspace is a linear subspace exactly when it contains $0$.
links.why: It shows that a linear subspace is an affine subspace through the origin, and that affine ones are translates.

reminder: In an algebraic extension, every element is a root of a nonzero polynomial over the base field.
definition: A [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ is algebraic when every element of $L$ is a [root](c:root) of a nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) with coefficients in $K$. Equivalently, every element of $L$ is an [algebraic element](c:algebraic-element) over $K$.
examples: $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is algebraic, because each $a+bi$ is a root of $x^2-2ax+a^2+b^2$.
$\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$ is algebraic. Every finite extension is algebraic.
Non-example: $\mathbb R/\mathbb Q$ is not algebraic, because $\pi$ is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients.

steps: Take an algebraic extension $L/K$.
It is a [field extension](c:field-extension), because $K$ is a subfield of $L$.
The algebraic case adds that each element of $L$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial over $K$.
links.why: It shows that algebraic is a condition on elements, not on the size of the extension.

steps: Take a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) $L/K$, which is algebraic, normal and separable.
Forget normality and separability.
What remains is that every element of $L$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial over $K$.
links.why: It shows that Galois extensions are algebraic extensions with two more conditions.

reminder: An algebraic space is a sheaf with representable diagonal that has an étale atlas by a scheme.
definition: An algebraic space is a [sheaf](c:sheaf) $X$ on the [fppf site](c:fppf-site) of [schemes](c:scheme) such that the diagonal $X\to X\times X$ is a [representable morphism](c:representable-morphism) and there is a scheme $U$ with an [étale](c:etale-morphism-of-schemes) surjection $U\to X$. The scheme $U$ is an atlas of $X$.
examples: Every scheme is an algebraic space.
The quotient of a scheme by a free action of a finite group is an algebraic space. It need not be a scheme.
Non-example: the classifying stack $B\mu_2$ is not an algebraic space, because it has non-trivial automorphism groups and is not a sheaf of sets.

steps: Take a [scheme](c:scheme) $X$ and the sheaf that it represents.
The diagonal of $X$ is an immersion, so it is representable.
The identity $X\to X$ is an étale surjection from a scheme.
Hence $X$ is an algebraic space.
links.why: It shows that algebraic spaces extend schemes by allowing étale-local gluing.

steps: View the sheaf $X$ as a stack by treating each set $X(T)$ as a discrete groupoid.
The diagonal is representable and an étale atlas is smooth, so $X$ is an [algebraic stack](c:algebraic-stack).
The algebraic space case adds that every object has a trivial automorphism group.
links.why: It shows that an algebraic space is an algebraic stack without automorphisms.

reminder: An algorithm is a finite list of exact mechanical steps that gives an output for every input of a problem class.
definition: An algorithm is a finite set of exact instructions that a person or a machine follows without any choice or guess. For each input from a class of problems, it stops after finitely many steps and gives the output that solves the problem. Its input and output are finite objects, and it computes a [function](c:function) from inputs to outputs.
examples: The [Euclidean algorithm](c:euclidean-algorithm) computes the greatest common divisor of two integers.
School long division, and merge sort on a [finite set](c:finite-set) of numbers, are algorithms.
Non-example: the instruction "guess a root of the polynomial" is not an algorithm, because it is not an exact mechanical procedure.

steps: Take two positive integers $a$ and $b$ as the input.
Replace $(a,b)$ by $(b,a \bmod b)$ until the second number is $0$.
Each step is exact and the second number decreases, so the process stops after finitely many steps.
The first number at the end is the output, so this is an algorithm for the greatest common divisor.
links.why: It shows one concrete algorithm that meets every clause of the definition.

reminder: The alternating group $A_n$ is the subgroup of even permutations in the symmetric group $S_n$.
definition: For $n\ge1$, the alternating group $A_n$ is the [subgroup](c:subgroup) of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$ that consists of the even [permutations](c:permutation). A permutation is even when it is a product of an even number of [transpositions](c:transposition). Equivalently, $A_n$ is the kernel of the sign map $S_n\to\{\pm1\}$.
examples: $A_3$ is cyclic of order $3$, generated by the cycle $(1\,2\,3)$.
$A_n$ has order $n!/2$ for $n\ge2$, so $A_4$ has order $12$ and $A_5$ has order $60$.
Non-example: the transposition $(1\,2)$ is not in $A_n$, because it is a product of one transposition, which is an odd number.

steps: Take $A_n\subseteq S_n$, so that each element is a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
The group law is composition of permutations, as in $S_n$.
So $A_n$ is a [permutation group](c:permutation-group).
The alternating case adds the condition that every permutation is even.
links.why: It shows that $A_n$ is a permutation group, and that evenness is the only extra condition.

reminder: An angle bisector is a ray from the vertex of an [angle](c:angle) that splits it into two equal angles.
definition: The bisector of an [angle](c:angle) with [vertex](c:vertex) $V$ is the ray from $V$ that makes equal angles with the two sides of the angle. In a [triangle](c:triangle), the bisector from a vertex is the [line segment](c:line-segment) from this vertex to the point where the bisecting ray meets the opposite side.
examples: In an equilateral triangle, each angle bisector is also a median and an altitude.
In triangle $ABC$, the bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $BD/DC=AB/AC$.
Non-example: a median of a triangle is not an angle bisector in general, because the midpoint of the opposite side splits that side but not the angle into equal parts.

reminder: The angle sum of a polygon is the total of its interior angles, and a plane triangle has angle sum $180^\circ$.
definition: The angle sum of a [polygon](c:polygon) is the sum of its interior [angles](c:angle). In the Euclidean plane, the angle sum of every [triangle](c:triangle) is $180^\circ$ ($\pi$ radians), and the angle sum of a convex $n$-gon is $(n-2)\cdot180^\circ$.
examples: A triangle with angles $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ has angle sum $180^\circ$.
Every convex quadrilateral has angle sum $360^\circ$.
Non-example: a spherical triangle with three right angles has angle sum $270^\circ$, so the value $180^\circ$ fails outside the Euclidean plane.

reminder: The arctangent of $x$ is the unique angle in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ whose tangent is $x$.
definition: The arctangent $\arctan:\mathbb R\to(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ is the [inverse function](c:inverse-function) of the [tangent function](c:tangent-function) restricted to $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$. It is increasing, [analytic](c:analytic-function), and satisfies $\arctan 0=0$ and $\arctan'(x)=1/(1+x^2)$.
examples: $\arctan 1=\pi/4$ and $\arctan 0=0$.
$\arctan x\to\pi/2$ as $x\to\infty$ and $\arctan x\to-\pi/2$ as $x\to-\infty$.
Non-example: $\arctan(\tan(3\pi/4))=-\pi/4$, not $3\pi/4$, because the arctangent only gives angles in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.

steps: The tangent is strictly increasing on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, so it is injective there.
An injective function has an inverse on its image, and the image of tangent here is $\mathbb R$.
This inverse is the arctangent, so it is an [inverse trigonometric function](c:inverse-trigonometric-function).
links.why: It shows that the arctangent is one inverse of a trigonometric function on a chosen branch.

steps: Restrict the tangent to the interval $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, where it is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$.
A bijection has a two-sided [inverse function](c:inverse-function).
The arctangent is this inverse, so $\tan(\arctan x)=x$ for every real $x$.
links.why: It shows that the arctangent is an inverse function on a restricted domain, and why the restriction is needed.

reminder: An arithmetic function is a complex-valued function defined on the positive integers.
definition: An arithmetic function is a [function](c:function) $f:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\mathbb C$ from the positive [natural numbers](c:natural-number) to the [complex numbers](c:complex-number). Number theory studies such functions through their values at primes and prime powers.
examples: Euler's totient function $\varphi(n)$ counts the integers from $1$ to $n$ that are coprime to $n$.
The divisor function $d(n)$, the number of positive divisors of $n$, and $\omega(n)$ are arithmetic functions.
Non-example: $\sin x$ on $\mathbb R$ is not an arithmetic function, because its domain is not the set of positive integers.

steps: Start with an arithmetic function $f$.
Add the condition $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ for all coprime positive integers $m$ and $n$.
Then $f$ is an [additive function](c:additive-function).
links.why: It shows that additive functions are the arithmetic functions that turn coprime products into sums.

reminder: The Artin map sends an ideal coprime to the ramified primes to the product of the Frobenius elements of its prime factors.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a finite [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) of [number fields](c:number-field). For a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $K$ that is [unramified](c:ramification-of-ideals) in $L$, the [Frobenius element](c:frobenius-element) $\mathrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak p}$ lies in the [Galois group](c:galois-group) $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$. The Artin map sends a fractional ideal $\prod\mathfrak p^{a_{\mathfrak p}}$, coprime to the ramified primes, to $\prod\mathrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak p}^{a_{\mathfrak p}}$.
examples: For $L=\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ and $K=\mathbb Q$, the Artin map sends a prime $p\nmid n$ to the class of $p$ in $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times\cong\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$.
For $L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$ with $d$ squarefree, an odd prime $p$ not dividing $d$ goes to the identity if $d$ is a square mod $p$, and to the non-trivial element otherwise.
Non-example: in a non-abelian Galois extension, a prime has only a conjugacy class of Frobenius elements, so there is no Artin map into the Galois group.

reminder: Two functions are asymptotically equivalent when the ratio of their values tends to $1$.
definition: For functions $f$ and $g$ with $g(x)\ne0$ for large $x$, write $f\sim g$ as $x\to\infty$ when $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)/g(x)=1$. This is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) on such functions. It uses the [limit of a function](c:limit-of-a-function).
examples: $x^2+x\sim x^2$ as $x\to\infty$.
Stirling's formula says $n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n$.
Non-example: $2x\not\sim x$, because the ratio $2x/x$ tends to $2$, not to $1$.

reminder: The augmentation ideal of an augmented algebra is the kernel of its augmentation map.
definition: Let $A$ be an [augmented algebra](c:augmented-algebra) over a ring $R$, with augmentation $\epsilon:A\to R$ a ring homomorphism that is the identity on $R$. The augmentation ideal is the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) $I=\ker\epsilon$, a two-sided [ideal](c:ideal) of $A$. It satisfies $A=R\cdot1\oplus I$.
examples: In the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $R[G]$ with $\epsilon(\sum a_gg)=\sum a_g$, the augmentation ideal is spanned by the elements $g-1$.
In $R[x]$ with $\epsilon(f)=f(0)$, the augmentation ideal is the ideal $(x)$.
Non-example: the whole algebra $A$ is not an augmentation ideal, because $\epsilon(1)=1\ne0$, so the unit is never in the kernel.

steps: The kernel of a ring homomorphism is a two-sided [ideal](c:ideal).
So $I=\ker\epsilon$ is an ideal of $A$.
The augmentation case adds that $\epsilon$ is the identity on $R$, so $A=R\cdot1\oplus I$.
links.why: It shows that the augmentation ideal is an ideal that is a complement of the scalars.

reminder: Full comprehension says that every property $P$ defines the set of all objects that satisfy $P$.
definition: In an [unsorted set theory](c:unsorted-set-theory), the axiom of full comprehension says that for every property $P(x)$ there is a [set](c:set) $\{x\mid P(x)\}$ whose elements are exactly the objects that satisfy $P$. This [axiom](c:axiom) is inconsistent, because $P(x)\equiv x\notin x$ gives Russell's paradox.
examples: The property $x=x$ gives the set of all objects, the universal set.
The property "$x$ is an even natural number" gives the set of even natural numbers.
Non-example: the axiom of separation is weaker. It only forms $\{x\in A\mid P(x)\}$ inside a given set $A$, so it does not give Russell's set.

steps: Take a [set](c:set) $A$ and a property $P$.
Apply full comprehension to the property $x\in A\wedge P(x)$.
The resulting set is $\{x\in A\mid P(x)\}$, which is the set that separation gives.
So full comprehension implies separation, which adds the bound $x\in A$ and so avoids Russell's paradox.
links.why: It shows what separation keeps of comprehension, and what it adds to avoid the paradox.

reminder: The bar construction $B(M,A,N)$ is the simplicial object whose $n$-th level is $M\otimes A^{\otimes n}\otimes N$.
definition: Let $A$ be a [monoid](c:monoid) in a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category), let $M$ be a right $A$-module and let $N$ be a left $A$-module. The bar construction $B(M,A,N)$ is the [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) with $B_n=M\otimes A^{\otimes n}\otimes N$. Its face maps use the action of $A$ on $M$ and on $N$ and the product of $A$.
examples: For a group $G$, the space $B(*,G,*)$ has $n$-simplices $G^n$, and its [geometric realization](c:geometric-realization) is the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$.
For an algebra $A$ over a field $k$ and $A$-modules $M$ and $N$, the complex built from $B(M,A,N)$ computes $\mathrm{Tor}^A(M,N)$.
Non-example: if the product on $A$ is not associative, the face maps do not satisfy the simplicial identities, so there is no simplicial object.

reminder: A basic open set $D(f)$ of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is the set of prime ideals that do not contain $f$.
definition: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $f\in A$. The basic open set is $D(f)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A\mid f\notin\mathfrak p\}$ in the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) of $A$. It is open in the [Zariski topology](c:zariski-topology), it is the [affine scheme](c:affine-scheme) of the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) $A_f$, and the sets $D(f)$ form a base of the topology.
examples: In $\mathbb A^1=\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$, the set $D(x)$ is $\mathbb A^1\setminus\{0\}=\operatorname{Spec}k[x,x^{-1}]$.
$D(1)$ is the whole space and $D(0)$ is empty.
Non-example: $\mathbb A^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ is open in $\operatorname{Spec}k[x,y]$ but is not a basic open set, because it is $D(x)\cup D(y)$ and its complement, a point, is not $V(f)$ for any $f$.

steps: The set $V(f)$ of prime ideals that contain $f$ is closed in the [Zariski topology](c:zariski-topology).
The set $D(f)$ is the complement of $V(f)$ in $\operatorname{Spec}A$.
So $D(f)$ is an [open set](c:open-set).
The basic case adds that every open set is a union of sets $D(f)$.
links.why: It shows that the basic open sets are the open sets that suffice to build the whole topology.

reminder: A basis of a vector space is a [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset) set of vectors that [spans](c:span) the space.
definition: A basis of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $k$ is a family $(b_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors that is [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset) and whose [span](c:span) is $V$. Equivalently, every vector of $V$ is a unique finite [linear combination](c:linear-combination) of the vectors $b_i$.
examples: The vectors $e_1,\dots,e_n$ form the standard basis of $k^n$.
The monomials $1,x,x^2,\dots$ form a basis of the space $k[x]$ of polynomials.
Non-example: the vectors $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ span $\mathbb R^2$ but are linearly dependent, so they are not a basis.

steps: A field $k$ is a ring, and a vector space over $k$ is a module over $k$.
Linear independence and spanning have the same meaning for modules as for vector spaces.
So a basis of $V$ is a basis of the module $V$, and $V$ is a [free module](c:free-module).
The vector space case adds that every module over a field has a basis.
links.why: It shows that a basis of a vector space is the field case of a basis of a free module, where freeness is automatic.

steps: Take a basis $B$ of $V$.
By definition, $B$ is [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset).
The basis case adds that $B$ spans $V$.
So $B$ is a maximal linearly independent set.
links.why: It shows that a basis is a linearly independent set that is as large as possible.

reminder: A behavior strategy gives, at each information set of a player, a probability distribution over the available actions.
definition: In an [extensive-form game](c:extensive-form-game), a behavior strategy of a player assigns to each information set of that player a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) over the actions available there. The player makes the random choices at different information sets independently.
examples: A player with one information set and actions $L$ and $R$ plays $L$ with probability $0.3$ and $R$ with probability $0.7$.
A pure strategy is a behavior strategy in which every distribution puts probability $1$ on one action.
Non-example: a mixed strategy is one random draw of a whole pure strategy before play, so it is a different object. Under [perfect recall](c:perfect-recall), both give the same outcomes.

reminder: The Beltrami equation $f_{\bar z}=\mu f_z$, with $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$, prescribes the local distortion of a [quasiconformal map](c:quasiconformal-map).
definition: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be an [open set](c:open-set) and let $\mu:U\to\mathbb C$ be a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) with $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$. The Beltrami equation is the [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation) $\partial f/\partial\bar z=\mu\,\partial f/\partial z$ for $f:U\to\mathbb C$. A homeomorphic solution in $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a [quasiconformal map](c:quasiconformal-map) with Beltrami coefficient $\mu$.
examples: For $\mu=0$, the equation is $f_{\bar z}=0$, and its solutions are the holomorphic functions.
For a constant $\mu=k$ with $|k|<1$, the map $f(z)=z+k\bar z$ solves the equation.
Non-example: for $\mu\equiv1$, the map $f=z+\bar z=2x$ solves the equation but squeezes the plane onto a line, so it is not a homeomorphism. This is why $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$ is required.

steps: Write $\partial_{\bar z}=\tfrac12(\partial_x+i\partial_y)$ for the derivative with respect to $\bar z$.
The [Cauchy-Riemann equations](c:cauchy-riemann-equations) for $f=u+iv$ say exactly that $\partial f/\partial\bar z=0$.
This is the Beltrami equation with $\mu=0$.
links.why: It shows that the Beltrami equation deforms the Cauchy-Riemann equation by a coefficient $\mu$.

reminder: The Bernoulli polynomial $B_n(x)$ is the coefficient of $t^n/n!$ in the expansion of $te^{xt}/(e^t-1)$.
definition: The Bernoulli polynomials $B_n(x)$ are the [polynomials](c:polynomial) defined by the [generating function](c:generating-function) $\frac{te^{xt}}{e^t-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}B_n(x)\frac{t^n}{n!}$. Each $B_n(x)$ has [rational](c:rational-number) coefficients, and $B_n(0)$ is the [Bernoulli number](c:bernoulli-number) $B_n$.
examples: $B_2(x)=x^2-x+\tfrac16$, and they sum powers: $\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}k^n=\dfrac{B_{n+1}(m)-B_{n+1}(0)}{n+1}$.
Non-example: $x^2-x+1$ is not $B_2(x)$, because its constant term is $1$ but $B_2(0)=\tfrac16$.

steps: Set $x=0$ in the generating function to get $t/(e^t-1)$.
The coefficients of $t^n/n!$ in this series are the [Bernoulli numbers](c:bernoulli-number) $B_n$.
So $B_n(0)=B_n$, and each Bernoulli number is a value of a Bernoulli polynomial.
links.why: It shows that the polynomials are a family in $x$ whose value at $0$ is the Bernoulli number.

reminder: Beta-reduction rewrites $(\lambda x.M)\,N$ to $M[N/x]$, which is $M$ with $N$ put in place of $x$.
definition: In the [lambda calculus](c:lambda-calculus), $\beta$-reduction rewrites a redex $(\lambda x.M)\,N$ to the [term](c:term) $M[N/x]$. This term is $M$ with $N$ substituted for the free occurrences of $x$, after bound variables are renamed to avoid capture, as [alpha-equivalence](c:alpha-equivalence) allows. The rewrite may apply to any subterm.
examples: $(\lambda x.x)\,y\to y$.
$(\lambda x.\lambda y.x)\,a\,b\to(\lambda y.a)\,b\to a$.
Non-example: $(\lambda x.\lambda y.x)\,y\to\lambda y.y$ is not a correct step, because the free $y$ is captured. Rename the bound variable first to get $\lambda z.y$.

steps: A [conversion rule](c:conversion-rule) says that two terms are equal, so one may replace the other.
The rule $(\lambda x.M)\,N=M[N/x]$ equates a redex with its contraction.
Read from left to right, it replaces a more complicated term by a simpler one.
So $\beta$-reduction is the conversion rule of computation.
links.why: It shows that beta-reduction is the conversion rule that carries out computation.

reminder: The bidual of a normed space $X$ is $X^{**}$, the dual of its dual space $X^*$.
definition: The bidual of a [normed space](c:normed-space) $X$ is the [dual space](c:dual-space) of its dual, $X^{**}=(X^*)^*$, with the dual norm. The canonical map $J:X\to X^{**}$, $J(x)(\varphi)=\varphi(x)$, is a linear isometric embedding.
examples: For a finite-dimensional $X$, the canonical map $J$ is an isomorphism, so $X^{**}\cong X$.
For $X=c_0$, the bidual $c_0^{**}$ is $\ell^\infty$.
Non-example: the space $c_0$ is not its own bidual, because $c_0^{**}=\ell^\infty$ is strictly larger and $J$ is not onto.

steps: Take the [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$ of continuous linear functionals on $X$, with the operator norm.
The space $X^*$ is again a normed space, so it has a dual space.
That dual space of $X^*$ is the bidual $X^{**}$.
links.why: It shows that the bidual is the dual construction applied twice.

reminder: A biholomorphic function is a holomorphic bijection whose inverse is also holomorphic.
definition: A function $f:U\to V$ between open subsets of $\mathbb C$ (or between complex manifolds) is biholomorphic when it is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) and a [bijection](c:bijection) whose [inverse function](c:inverse-function) is also holomorphic.
examples: The Cayley transform $z\mapsto(z-i)/(z+i)$ is a biholomorphic map from the upper half-plane onto the unit disk.
Every Möbius transformation is a biholomorphic map of the Riemann sphere.
Non-example: $z\mapsto z^2$ on $\mathbb C$ is holomorphic but not injective, so it is not biholomorphic.

steps: Take a biholomorphic function $f:U\to V$.
By definition, $f$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function).
The biholomorphic case adds that $f$ is a bijection and that $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic.
links.why: It shows that biholomorphic is holomorphic plus a holomorphic inverse.

steps: Let $f:U\to V$ be biholomorphic with inverse $g$.
The chain rule on $g(f(z))=z$ gives $g'(f(z))\,f'(z)=1$, so $f'(z)\ne0$.
A holomorphic function with non-zero derivative preserves oriented angles.
So $f$ is a [conformal map](c:conformal-map) that is also a bijection.
links.why: It shows that a biholomorphic map keeps angles, so it is a conformal map in one complex variable.

steps: Take the category with complex manifolds as objects and holomorphic maps as morphisms.
An isomorphism is a morphism $f$ that has a two-sided inverse morphism $g$.
Here $f$ and $g$ are holomorphic maps with $g\circ f$ and $f\circ g$ equal to the identity.
So the [isomorphisms](c:isomorphism) of this category are exactly the biholomorphic functions.
links.why: It shows that biholomorphic functions are the isomorphisms of complex geometry.

reminder: An $(R,S)$-bimodule is an abelian group with a left $R$-action and a right $S$-action that commute.
definition: Let $R$ and $S$ be [rings](c:ring). An $(R,S)$-bimodule is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $M$ that is a left [module](c:module) over $R$ and a right module over $S$, and that satisfies $(rm)s=r(ms)$ for all $r\in R$, $m\in M$ and $s\in S$.
examples: A ring $R$ is an $(R,R)$-bimodule when it acts on itself by multiplication on both sides.
The matrices $M_{m\times n}(k)$ form an $(M_m(k),M_n(k))$-bimodule.
Non-example: a left module $M$ over a non-commutative ring $R$ does not become a right module by $m\cdot r:=rm$, because $m\cdot(rs)=rsm$ but $(m\cdot r)\cdot s=srm$.

steps: Take a left [module](c:module) $M$ over a ring $R$.
Every abelian group is a right module over $\mathbb Z$ in exactly one way.
The left $R$-action and the right $\mathbb Z$-action commute.
So $M$ is an $(R,\mathbb Z)$-bimodule.
links.why: It shows that every module is a bimodule, and that a bimodule adds a second commuting action.

reminder: The binomial distribution $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ counts the successes in $n$ independent trials that each succeed with probability $p$.
definition: Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and $p\in[0,1]$. The binomial distribution $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) of the number $X$ of successes in $n$ [independent](c:independent-random-variables) trials with success probability $p$ each. It satisfies $P(X=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ for $k=0,\dots,n$, with the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) $\binom nk$.
examples: The number of heads in $10$ tosses of a fair coin has distribution $\mathrm{Bin}(10,1/2)$.
The number of defective items among $n$ items that fail independently with probability $p$ has distribution $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$.
Non-example: the number of red balls in $5$ draws without replacement from an urn is hypergeometric, not binomial, because the draws are not independent.

steps: Take $n=1$ in $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$.
Then $P(X=1)=p$ and $P(X=0)=1-p$.
This is the [Bernoulli distribution](c:bernoulli-distribution) with parameter $p$.
In general, $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ is the law of a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli variables.
links.why: It shows that the binomial law is the sum of independent coin flips, and that $n=1$ is a single flip.

reminder: A birational map is a rational map with a rational inverse, so it is an isomorphism between dense open subsets.
definition: A [rational map](c:rational-map) $f:X\dashrightarrow Y$ of [varieties](c:algebraic-variety) is birational when there is a rational map $g:Y\dashrightarrow X$ with $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_X$ and $f\circ g=\mathrm{id}_Y$ as rational maps. Equivalently, $f$ restricts to an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) between [dense](c:dense-set) open subsets of $X$ and $Y$.
examples: The map $t\mapsto(t^2-1,\,t(t^2-1))$ is a birational map from $\mathbb A^1$ to the nodal cubic $y^2=x^2(x+1)$, with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto y/x$.
The blow-up of a smooth surface at a point is a birational map onto the surface.
Non-example: the map $\mathbb A^1\to\mathbb A^1$, $x\mapsto x^2$ is not birational, because a general point has two preimages and so there is no rational inverse.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) of varieties with inverse $g$.
Regular maps are rational maps, so $f$ and $g$ are rational maps.
They satisfy $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}_X$ and $f\circ g=\mathrm{id}_Y$.
So $f$ is birational, but the converse fails, because a birational map may be undefined at some points.
links.why: It shows that birational maps are isomorphisms that may fail on a small closed set.

steps: A [birational morphism](c:birational-morphism) is a morphism $f:X\to Y$ that is also birational.
A morphism is a rational map that is defined at every point of $X$.
So $f$ is a birational map.
The morphism case adds the condition that $f$ is defined everywhere.
links.why: It shows that a birational morphism is a birational map with no points of indeterminacy.

reminder: A block design is a set of points with blocks such that every pair of points lies in the same number of blocks.
definition: A block 2-design of type $(v,\beta,r,k,\lambda)$ consists of a [set](c:set) of $v$ points and a family of $\beta$ blocks, each block a [subset](c:subset) of $k$ points. Every point lies in exactly $r$ blocks, and every pair of distinct points lies in exactly $\lambda$ blocks.
examples: The Fano plane has $7$ points and $7$ lines of $3$ points each, and every pair of points lies on exactly one line. It is a design of type $(7,7,3,3,1)$.
All $2$-element subsets of a $v$-element set form a design with $k=2$, $\lambda=1$, $\beta=\binom v2$ and $r=v-1$.
Non-example: on the points $1,2,3,4$ the blocks $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{1,2,4\}$ and $\{1,3,4\}$ do not form a design, because the pair $\{1,2\}$ lies in two blocks but the pair $\{2,3\}$ lies in one.

steps: Take a [Steiner system](c:steiner-system) $S(2,k,v)$, in which each pair of the $v$ points lies in exactly one block of size $k$.
Give the parameter $\lambda$ the value $1$ for every pair of points.
Counting the blocks through one point gives the constant $r=(v-1)/(k-1)$, so every point lies in the same number of blocks.
So the blocks form a block 2-design, and the Steiner case adds the condition $\lambda=1$.
links.why: It shows that a Steiner system with $t=2$ is a block design with $\lambda=1$.

reminder: The blow-up of $X$ along $Z$ replaces $Z$ by a divisor of normal directions and does not change $X\setminus Z$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [scheme](c:scheme) and let $\mathcal I$ be a [sheaf of ideals](c:sheaf-of-ideals) that defines a closed subscheme $Z$. The blow-up of $X$ along $Z$ is $\mathrm{Bl}_ZX=\operatorname{Proj}\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathcal I^n$ with its map $\pi:\mathrm{Bl}_ZX\to X$, built with the [projective spectrum](c:projective-spectrum) construction. Over $X\setminus Z$ the map $\pi$ is an isomorphism, and $\pi^{-1}(Z)$ is a Cartier divisor, the exceptional divisor.
examples: The blow-up of $\mathbb A^2$ at the origin is $\{((x,y),[u:v])\mid xv=yu\}\subseteq\mathbb A^2\times\mathbb P^1$, and the origin becomes the line $\mathbb P^1$.
Blowing up a point of a smooth surface replaces the point by a projective line.
Non-example: the projection $\mathbb A^2\to\mathbb A^1$ is not a blow-up, because it is not an isomorphism outside a proper closed subset, since its fibres are lines.

steps: Let $X$ be an integral scheme and $Z$ a proper closed subscheme, with blow-up $\pi:\mathrm{Bl}_ZX\to X$.
Over the dense open set $X\setminus Z$, the map $\pi$ is an isomorphism.
The blow-up is integral too, so $\pi^{-1}(X\setminus Z)$ is dense in it.
Hence $\pi$ is a [birational morphism](c:birational-morphism).
links.why: It shows that a blow-up changes a variety only along $Z$, so it never changes the function field.

reminder: A Blum complexity measure assigns a cost $\Phi_e(x)$ that is defined exactly when program $e$ halts on $x$, and the statement $\Phi_e(x)=y$ is decidable.
definition: Fix an acceptable numbering $\varphi_e$ of the [partial computable functions](c:partial-computable-function). A Blum complexity measure is a family of partial computable functions $\Phi_e$ such that $\Phi_e(x)$ is defined exactly when $\varphi_e(x)$ is defined. In addition, the relation $\Phi_e(x)=y$ must be [decidable](c:computable-set) in $e$, $x$ and $y$.
examples: The number of steps that the [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $e$ makes on input $x$ is a Blum measure. It is defined exactly when the machine halts, and one decides whether it equals $y$ by running $y$ steps.
The number of tape cells that machine $e$ uses on input $x$ is also a Blum measure, with the usual convention for machines that loop.
Non-example: $\Phi_e(x)=0$ for all $e$ and $x$ is not a Blum measure, because it is defined even when $\varphi_e(x)$ diverges.

reminder: The Boltzmann distribution gives a state with energy $E$ a probability proportional to $e^{-E/(k_BT)}$.
definition: Let a system have states $i$ with energies $E_i$, and let $\beta=1/(k_BT)$ for the temperature $T$. The Boltzmann distribution is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $p_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$, where the [partition function](c:partition-function) is $Z=\sum_ie^{-\beta E_i}$. Among all distributions with a fixed [expectation value](c:expectation-value) of the energy, it has the largest [entropy](c:entropy).
examples: A two-level system with energies $0$ and $\varepsilon$ is in the upper level with probability $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})$.
The velocity of a molecule in a classical gas follows the Maxwell-Boltzmann law, which is a Boltzmann distribution in the kinetic energy.
Non-example: a uniform distribution on states with different energies is not a Boltzmann distribution at any finite temperature, because lower energies must have larger probability.

steps: Take finitely many states $i$ with energies $E_i$ and a number $\beta$.
The weights $e^{-\beta E_i}$ are positive.
Divide each weight by their sum $Z$, so that the total probability is $1$.
The result is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) in which each probability depends only on the energy.
links.why: It shows that the Boltzmann law is a probability distribution built from energy weights.

reminder: A boundary point of a set $S$ is a point whose every neighborhood meets both $S$ and its complement.
definition: Let $S$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. A point $x\in X$ is a boundary point of $S$ when every [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) of $x$ contains a point of $S$ and a point outside $S$. The set of all boundary points is the [boundary](c:boundary) of $S$.
examples: The points $0$ and $1$ are boundary points of the interval $(0,1)$ in $\mathbb R$.
Every point of the unit circle is a boundary point of the open unit disk in $\mathbb R^2$.
Non-example: the point $1/2$ is not a boundary point of $[0,1]$, because the neighborhood $(0.4,0.6)$ lies inside $[0,1]$.

reminder: A distribution is bracket-generating when its vector fields and their iterated Lie brackets span the tangent space at every point.
definition: Let $D$ be a [distribution](c:distribution-of-subspaces) on a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$, that is a choice of a subspace $D_x\subseteq T_xM$ at each point $x$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the [vector fields](c:vector-field) tangent to $D$. The distribution $D$ is bracket-generating when the fields in $\mathcal D$ together with their iterated [Lie brackets](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields) span $T_xM$ at every point $x$.
examples: On $\mathbb R^3$, the fields $X=\partial_x-\tfrac y2\partial_z$ and $Y=\partial_y+\tfrac x2\partial_z$ span a distribution with $[X,Y]=\partial_z$, so $X$, $Y$ and $[X,Y]$ span the tangent space at every point.
The whole tangent bundle $D=TM$ is bracket-generating, with no brackets needed.
Non-example: the distribution spanned by $\partial_x$ on $\mathbb R^2$ is not bracket-generating, because brackets of fields $f\partial_x$ stay multiples of $\partial_x$ and never give $\partial_y$.

steps: Start with a [distribution](c:distribution-of-subspaces) $D$ on $M$ and set $D^1=D$.
Let $D^{k+1}$ be spanned by $D^k$ and all brackets $[X,Y]$ with $X$ a section of $D$ and $Y$ a section of $D^k$.
The bracket-generating case adds the condition that $D^k_x=T_xM$ for some $k$ at every point $x$.
links.why: It shows that bracket-generating is a condition on the distribution that says brackets reach every direction.

reminder: A Cauchy filter is a proper filter that contains sets of arbitrarily small diameter.
definition: A [filter](c:filter) $\mathcal F$ on a [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ is Cauchy when it is proper and, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it contains a set of [diameter](c:diameter) less than $\varepsilon$. Here proper means that $\mathcal F$ does not contain the empty set.
examples: For a Cauchy sequence $(x_n)$, the filter generated by the tails $\{x_n\mid n\ge N\}$ is a Cauchy filter.
The neighborhood filter of a point of a metric space is a Cauchy filter, because it contains balls of radius $\varepsilon$ with diameter at most $2\varepsilon$.
Non-example: the filter generated by the tails of $x_n=n$ in $\mathbb R$ is not Cauchy, because every tail is unbounded and has infinite diameter.

steps: Take a sequence $(x_n)$ and let $\mathcal F$ be the filter generated by its tails $T_N=\{x_n\mid n\ge N\}$.
This filter is proper, because each tail is not empty.
The sequence is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) exactly when, for each $\varepsilon>0$, some tail has diameter at most $\varepsilon$.
So $(x_n)$ is Cauchy exactly when its tail filter is a Cauchy filter.
links.why: It shows that a Cauchy filter is the filter version of a Cauchy sequence.

reminder: A central charge is a generator of a central extension of a symmetry Lie algebra, and it usually acts as a number.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) of symmetries and let $\hat{\mathfrak g}$ be a [central extension](c:central-extension) of $\mathfrak g$ by an abelian Lie algebra $\mathfrak z$. The elements of $\mathfrak z$ commute with all of $\hat{\mathfrak g}$, and they are called central charges. In an irreducible representation, a central charge usually acts as a scalar.
examples: In the [Virasoro algebra](c:virasoro-algebra), $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}+\frac{c}{12}m(m^2-1)\delta_{m+n,0}$, and the number $c$ is the central charge.
A free boson has central charge $c=1$.
Non-example: $L_0$ in the Virasoro algebra is not a central charge, because $[L_0,L_n]=-nL_n$ is not zero for $n\ne0$.

reminder: A chain homotopy equivalence is a chain map that has an inverse chain map up to chain homotopy.
definition: A [chain map](c:chain-map) $f:C\to D$ of [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) is a chain homotopy equivalence when there is a chain map $g:D\to C$ such that $g\circ f$ and $f\circ g$ are [chain homotopic](c:chain-homotopy) to the identity maps of $C$ and $D$. The map $g$ is then a homotopy inverse of $f$.
examples: Every isomorphism of chain complexes is a chain homotopy equivalence.
A homotopy equivalence of spaces $X\to Y$ induces a chain homotopy equivalence of singular chain complexes $C_*(X)\to C_*(Y)$.

Non-example: the projection from the complex $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z$ (in degrees $1$ and $0$) onto $\mathbb Z/2$ in degree $0$ is a quasi-isomorphism but not a chain homotopy equivalence, because every chain map back is zero.

steps: Take a chain homotopy equivalence $f:C\to D$.
By definition, $f$ is a [chain map](c:chain-map).
The special case adds a chain map $g:D\to C$ with $gf$ and $fg$ chain homotopic to the identities.
links.why: It shows that a chain homotopy equivalence is a chain map with an inverse up to homotopy.

steps: Let $f$ be a chain homotopy equivalence with homotopy inverse $g$.
Chain homotopic maps induce the same map on homology.
So $H(g)\circ H(f)$ and $H(f)\circ H(g)$ are identities.
Hence $f$ induces isomorphisms in homology, and so it is a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism).
links.why: It shows that every chain homotopy equivalence is a quasi-isomorphism, but not conversely.

steps: Let $f$ be an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) of chain complexes with inverse $g$.
Then $g\circ f$ and $f\circ g$ are equal to the identities.
The zero map is a chain homotopy between an identity and itself.
So $f$ is a chain homotopy equivalence.
links.why: It shows that chain homotopy equivalence relaxes equality of composites to homotopy.

reminder: A chain map between chain complexes is a family of maps $f_n$ that commute with the differentials.
definition: A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ between [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) is a family of [homomorphisms](c:homomorphism) $f_n:C_n\to D_n$ such that $d^D_n\circ f_n=f_{n-1}\circ d^C_n$ for all $n$. In words, $f$ commutes with the differentials.
examples: The identity map and the zero map of a chain complex are chain maps.
A continuous map $X\to Y$ induces a chain map $C_*(X)\to C_*(Y)$ of singular chain complexes.
Non-example: on the complex with $C_1=C_0=\mathbb Z$ and $d=2$, the maps $f_1=\mathrm{id}$ and $f_0=0$ are not a chain map, because $d f_1(1)=2$ but $f_0 d(1)=0$.

steps: Regard a chain complex as a graded module with a differential $d$ of degree $-1$.
A [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) of graded modules of degree $0$ is a family of maps $f_n:C_n\to D_n$.
The chain map case adds the condition that $f$ commutes with the differential.
links.why: It shows that a chain map is a homomorphism of graded modules that respects the differential.

steps: Start with a [chain homotopy equivalence](c:chain-homotopy-equivalence) $f:C\to D$.
Forget its homotopy inverse and the chain homotopies.
What remains is the chain map $f$.
links.why: It shows that chain maps are the morphisms, and homotopy equivalences are the invertible ones up to homotopy.

reminder: The capacity of a channel is the maximum of the [mutual information](c:mutual-information) between input and output over all input distributions.
definition: For a discrete memoryless channel with input $X$, output $Y$ and transition probabilities $p(y\mid x)$, the capacity is $C=\max_{p(x)}I(X;Y)$. Here $I(X;Y)$ is the [mutual information](c:mutual-information), and the maximum runs over all input [probability distributions](c:probability-distribution).
examples: A binary symmetric channel with flip probability $p$ has capacity $C=1-H_2(p)$ bits per use.
A binary erasure channel with erasure probability $\epsilon$ has capacity $1-\epsilon$.
Non-example: for a binary symmetric channel with $0<p<1/2$, the mutual information with input $P(X=1)=0.9$ is smaller than the capacity $1-H_2(p)$.

reminder: A characteristic element $w$ of an integral lattice satisfies $x\cdot x\equiv x\cdot w\pmod 2$ for every lattice vector $x$.
definition: Let $L$ be an [integral lattice](c:integral-lattice) with a symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$. An element $w\in L$ is characteristic when $\langle x,x\rangle\equiv\langle x,w\rangle\pmod2$ for all $x\in L$. In a [unimodular lattice](c:unimodular-lattice), characteristic elements exist and form one coset of $2L$.
examples: In $\mathbb Z^n$ with the standard form, $w=(1,\dots,1)$ is characteristic, because $\sum x_i^2\equiv\sum x_i\pmod2$.
In an even unimodular lattice, $w=0$ is characteristic, because every $x\cdot x$ is even.
Non-example: $w=0$ is not characteristic in $\mathbb Z^n$, because $x=e_1$ gives $x\cdot x=1\not\equiv0\pmod2$.

reminder: A choice function for a set picks one element from each nonempty subset of the set.
definition: Let $A$ be a [set](c:set). A choice function for $A$ is a [function](c:function) $f$ from the nonempty subsets of $A$ to $A$ such that $f(S)\in S$ for every nonempty subset $S$. Its domain is the [power set](c:power-set) of $A$ without the [empty subset](c:empty-subset).
examples: On $A=\mathbb N$, the function $S\mapsto\min S$ is a choice function.
For $A=\mathbb R$, the existence of a choice function cannot be proved without the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice).
Non-example: $S\mapsto\min S$ is not a choice function for $\mathbb R$, because the subset $(0,1)$ has no minimum.

reminder: The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_k(X)$ is the group of $k$-dimensional algebraic cycles on $X$ modulo rational equivalence.
definition: Let $X$ be a [scheme](c:scheme) of finite type over a field. The group $Z_k(X)$ of [algebraic cycles](c:algebraic-cycle) is the free abelian group on the closed integral subschemes of dimension $k$. The Chow group $\mathrm{CH}_k(X)$ is the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) of $Z_k(X)$ by [rational equivalence](c:rational-equivalence).
examples: $\mathrm{CH}_k(\mathbb P^n)\cong\mathbb Z$ for $0\le k\le n$, generated by the class of a linear subspace of dimension $k$.
For a smooth variety $X$, the group $\mathrm{CH}^1(X)$ is the divisor class group $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$.
Non-example: the group $Z_0(\mathbb P^1)$ of cycles is not the Chow group, because two distinct points stay different in $Z_0(\mathbb P^1)$ but have the same class in $\mathrm{CH}_0(\mathbb P^1)$.

reminder: A class function on a group $G$ is a function that is constant on each conjugacy class.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group). A class function on $G$ is a [function](c:function) $f:G\to k$ with $f(ghg^{-1})=f(h)$ for all $g,h\in G$. Equivalently, $f$ is constant on each [conjugacy class](c:conjugacy-class).
examples: The trace and the determinant are class functions on the group $GL_n(k)$.
Every function on an abelian group is a class function, because each conjugacy class is a single element.
Non-example: on $S_3$, the function $f(\sigma)=\sigma(1)$ is not a class function, because $(1\,2)$ and $(2\,3)$ are conjugate but $f$ takes the values $2$ and $1$.

steps: Let $\rho:G\to GL(V)$ be a representation with [character](c:character-of-a-representation) $\chi(g)=\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$.
The trace is invariant under conjugation, so $\chi(ghg^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(g)\rho(h)\rho(g)^{-1})=\chi(h)$.
So $\chi$ is constant on conjugacy classes.
Hence every character is a class function.
links.why: It shows that characters are class functions that come from representations.

reminder: The Clifford algebra of $(V,Q)$ is the associative algebra generated by $V$ with the relation $v^2=Q(v)$.
definition: Let $V$ be a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a field $k$ with a [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $Q$. The Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ is the quotient of the [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra) $T(V)$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the elements $v\otimes v-Q(v)\cdot1$ for $v\in V$. It is the universal associative [algebra over a field](c:algebra-over-a-field) generated by $V$ with $v^2=Q(v)$.
examples: For $Q=0$, the Clifford algebra is the [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) of $V$.
For $V=\mathbb R$ with $Q(x)=-x^2$, the Clifford algebra is $\mathbb C$. For $V=\mathbb R^2$ with $Q(x,y)=-x^2-y^2$, it is the quaternions.
Non-example: the polynomial algebra $k[x]$ is not the Clifford algebra of a finite-dimensional space, because $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ has the finite dimension $2^{\dim V}$.

steps: Take $Q=0$, the zero quadratic form.
The defining relation becomes $v^2=0$ for every $v\in V$.
This is the relation that defines the [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) $\Lambda V$ as a quotient of $T(V)$.
So $\mathrm{Cl}(V,0)$ equals $\Lambda V$ for every vector space $V$.
links.why: It shows that a Clifford algebra deforms the exterior algebra by a quadratic form.

reminder: A closed curve is a continuous map from an interval whose two end points have the same image.
definition: A closed curve in a space $X$ is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$ on a [closed interval](c:closed-interval) with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. Equivalently, it is a continuous map from the [circle](c:circle) to $X$. It may cross itself.
examples: The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ is a closed curve, which runs once around the unit circle.
The figure eight, run once, is a closed curve that crosses itself.
Non-example: the spiral $t\mapsto(t\cos t,t\sin t)$ on $[0,4\pi]$ is not closed, because $\gamma(0)=(0,0)$ but $\gamma(4\pi)=(4\pi,0)$.

steps: Take a closed curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$.
Add the condition that $\gamma(s)\ne\gamma(t)$ whenever $a\le s<t<b$.
A closed curve with this condition has no self-crossing, so it is a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve).
links.why: It shows that a simple closed curve is a closed curve that does not cross itself.

reminder: The closed interval $[a,b]$ is the set of real numbers $x$ with $a\le x\le b$.
definition: For [real numbers](c:real-number) $a\le b$, the closed interval is $[a,b]=\{x\in\mathbb R\mid a\le x\le b\}$. It contains both of its end points.
examples: The unit interval $[0,1]$ is a closed interval.
$[a,a]=\{a\}$ is a closed interval with one point.
Non-example: $(0,1]$ is not a closed interval, because it does not contain the end point $0$.

steps: An [interval](c:interval) is a set $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ such that $a<c<b$ with $a,b\in I$ implies $c\in I$.
The set $[a,b]$ has this property.
So $[a,b]$ is an interval.
The closed case adds that it contains both end points $a$ and $b$.
links.why: It shows that a closed interval is an interval that includes its end points.

reminder: A closed oriented manifold is a compact manifold without boundary together with a choice of orientation.
definition: A closed oriented manifold is a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold), that is a compact [manifold](c:manifold) without boundary, together with a choice of [orientation](c:orientation-of-a-manifold). Each closed oriented manifold $M$ of dimension $n$ has a [fundamental class](c:fundamental-class) in $H_n(M;\mathbb Z)$.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ with its standard orientation is a closed oriented manifold.
The torus $T^2$ and the surface of any genus $g$ are closed oriented manifolds, and so is $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with the orientation from its complex structure.
Non-example: the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$ is closed but not orientable. The closed disk is orientable but has a boundary.

steps: Take a closed oriented manifold $M$.
Forget the choice of orientation on $M$.
What remains is a compact manifold without boundary, a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold).
The oriented case adds a choice of orientation, which exists only when $M$ is orientable.
links.why: It shows that an orientation is the extra choice that a closed manifold needs for Poincaré duality over the integers.

reminder: A cocycle is an element $c$ of a cochain group whose coboundary $dc$ is zero.
definition: In a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) $(C^\bullet,d)$, an $n$-cocycle is a [cochain](c:cochain) $c\in C^n$ with $dc=0$. The cocycles form the group $Z^n=\ker d$, and the [cohomology](c:cohomology) group is $Z^n$ modulo the coboundaries $dC^{n-1}$.
examples: A closed [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$, with $d\omega=0$, is a cocycle of the de Rham complex.
For a group $G$ that acts trivially on $A$, a $1$-cocycle is a group homomorphism $G\to A$.
Non-example: the constant function $c(g)=1$ on a group $G$ with trivial action on $\mathbb Z$ is not a $1$-cocycle, because $c(gh)=1$ but $c(g)+c(h)=2$.

steps: Let $G$ act on an abelian group $A$ and use the standard [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) of $G$ with values in $A$.
A $1$-cochain is a map $c:G\to A$, and its coboundary is $(dc)(g,h)=g\cdot c(h)-c(gh)+c(g)$.
So $dc=0$ exactly when $c(gh)=c(g)+g\cdot c(h)$ for all $g,h$.
Hence the $1$-cocycles of group cohomology are exactly the [crossed homomorphisms](c:crossed-homomorphism).
links.why: It shows that the identity for crossed homomorphisms is the cocycle condition in degree one.

reminder: A coherent state is the image of a fixed reference vector under the action of a group on a Hilbert space.
definition: Let $\pi$ be an irreducible [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) of a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$, and fix a unit vector $\psi_0\in H$. The coherent states are the vectors $\pi(g)\psi_0$ for $g\in G$, taken up to a phase. Under mild conditions they form an overcomplete family in $H$.
examples: For the [harmonic oscillator](c:harmonic-oscillator), the vectors $|\alpha\rangle=e^{-|\alpha|^2/2}\sum_n\frac{\alpha^n}{\sqrt{n!}}|n\rangle$ are coherent states, and they satisfy $a|\alpha\rangle=\alpha|\alpha\rangle$.
For $SU(2)$ acting on a spin-$j$ space, the orbit of the highest weight vector gives the spin coherent states.
Non-example: the number state $|n\rangle$ with $n\ge1$ is not a coherent state of the oscillator, because $a|n\rangle=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle$ is not a multiple of $|n\rangle$.

reminder: The comma category of $F$ and $G$ has as objects the morphisms $F(c)\to G(d)$ of the target category.
definition: Let $F:C\to E$ and $G:D\to E$ be [functors](c:functor) into the same [category](c:category). The comma category $(F\downarrow G)$ has as objects the triples $(c,d,h)$ with $h:F(c)\to G(d)$ a morphism of $E$. A morphism $(c,d,h)\to(c',d',h')$ is a pair $(u:c\to c',\,v:d\to d')$ with $h'\circ F(u)=G(v)\circ h$.
examples: If $F=G=\mathrm{id}_E$, then $(F\downarrow G)$ is the [arrow category](c:arrow-category) of $E$.
If $E$ is the terminal category, then $(F\downarrow G)$ is the product category $C\times D$.
Non-example: functors $F:C\to E$ and $G:D\to E'$ into different categories $E\ne E'$ have no comma category, because $h:F(c)\to G(d)$ needs a common target.

steps: Let $e$ be an object of $E$, and let $e:1\to E$ be the functor from the terminal category that picks it out.
Form the comma category of $\mathrm{id}_E$ and $e$.
Its objects are the morphisms $x\to e$, and its morphisms are commuting triangles.
That is the [over category](c:over-category) $E/e$.
links.why: It shows that slice categories are comma categories with one functor fixed to a point.

steps: Take $F=G=\mathrm{id}_E$ for a category $E$.
An object of $(F\downarrow G)$ is then a morphism $h:x\to y$ of $E$.
A morphism is a pair $(u,v)$ with $h'\circ u=v\circ h$, which is a commuting square.
This is the [arrow category](c:arrow-category) of $E$.
links.why: It shows that the arrow category is the comma category of the identity functor with itself.

reminder: A category is complete when every small diagram in it has a limit.
definition: A [category](c:category) $C$ is complete when every functor $D\to C$ from a [small category](c:small-category) $D$ has a [limit](c:limit-category-theory) in $C$. In other words, every small [diagram](c:diagram) in $C$ has a limit.
examples: The categories of sets, groups, topological spaces and abelian groups are complete.
Every complete lattice, seen as a poset category, is a complete category.
Non-example: the category of finite sets is not complete, because the product of infinitely many copies of $\{0,1\}$ is not finite.

steps: Let $C$ be a complete category, so every small diagram in $C$ has a limit.
A finite diagram is a small diagram.
So every finite diagram in $C$ has a limit.
Hence $C$ is [finitely complete](c:finitely-complete-category), and the complete case adds limits of all small diagrams.
links.why: It shows that completeness strengthens finite completeness from finite diagrams to all small diagrams.

steps: Take a [bicomplete category](c:bicomplete-category), which has all small limits and all small colimits.
Ignore the colimits and keep only the limits.
What remains is that all small limits exist.
So every bicomplete category is complete.
links.why: It shows that a bicomplete category is a complete category that is also cocomplete.
